result: Human participants achieved 77.94% accuracy on the reading comprehension task, while simple heuristic models (orthographic: 25.6%, semantic: 27.3%) and the SAR model (47.6%) performed poorly. Transformer-based models achieved 37.08% accuracy after pre-training and 73% after fine-tuning, approaching human performance.
evaluation: Claims C16-C21 provide converging evidence from human behavioral data and computational model performance. The low accuracy of simple models (C17-C19) demonstrates task complexity, while transformer models' improvement with fine-tuning (C21) shows they can approach human-level performance (C16). All claims are supported by data presented in Figure 1B.

result: Participants in Experiment 1 read passages at 457±142 words/min, approximately twice the normal reading speed for native readers, indicating development of a specialized reading strategy for the goal-directed task.
evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are well-supported by experimental data (C22, C23) and comparison to established reading norms (C24). The inference that faster reading indicates a specialized strategy is reasonable given the task demands and is supported by Figure 1C data.

result: Transformer-based DNN attention weights predict human word reading time better than heuristic models or SAR. Predictive power increased from ~0.2 (heuristic models) to ~0.3 (random transformers) to ~0.5 (pre-trained transformers), with fine-tuning further boosting prediction for local but not global questions.
evaluation: Claims C25-C29 present a clear progression of model performance supported by correlation analyses and statistical testing (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1a). The differential effect of fine-tuning on local vs. global questions (C29) is particularly well-documented and adds specificity to the findings.

result: Layout and word features significantly predict word reading time, with layout features showing stronger effects for global than local questions. However, transformer-based model attention weights provide superior predictive power compared to these basic text features alone.
evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are supported by regression analyses (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1b) and linear mixed effects modeling (C33). The statistical comparisons (C31, C34) demonstrate both the contribution of text features and the additional explanatory power of DNN attention weights.

result: After controlling for layout, word features, and question relevance, transformer-based model attention weights still significantly predict residual word reading time (predictive power ~0.2-0.3), with more than 85% of DNN attention heads contributing to predictions.
evaluation: Claims C35-C38 demonstrate that DNN attention captures information beyond basic text and task features through systematic regression analyses (Figure 3—figure supplements 1B-C). The linear mixed effects model result (C38) provides additional statistical rigor, though the drop in predictive power suggests substantial overlap with measured features.

result: Question-relevant words show distinct spatial distributions: uniformly distributed for local questions but concentrated at passage beginnings for global questions. Readers allocate more reading time to passage beginnings for global questions and to lines with highest question relevance.
evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are well-supported by annotation data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B) and eye-tracking analyses (Figure 3C-D). The convergence between question relevance annotations and actual reading behavior strengthens the validity of both measures.

result: Human attention shows temporal dynamics: layout features increasingly influence late reading stages for global questions, word features remain stable across stages, while question relevance effects increase from early (gaze duration) to late (rereading) stages, suggesting hierarchical attention control.
evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by analysis of different eye-tracking measures (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1d). The inference about hierarchical control (C47) is reasonable given the temporal progression of effects, though alternative explanations are not explicitly ruled out.

result: DNN attention weights show layer-specific sensitivity: shallow layers are sensitive to word features across all model types, while deep layers are sensitive to question relevance only in fine-tuned models, indicating that goal-directed attention emerges through task-specific training.
evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by layer-wise regression analyses (Figure 4B-C, Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3). The parallel between human temporal dynamics and DNN layer hierarchy strengthens the computational account, though the inference about training-induced goal-directed attention (C50) could benefit from additional mechanistic evidence.

result: Experiment 2 (mixed question types) showed slower reading (298±123 words/min) than Experiment 1 (blocked design), with reduced question-type-specific effects. Fine-tuned models better predicted reading time than pre-trained models, but task modulation effects were weaker than in Experiment 1, indicating that blocked presentation facilitated development of question-type-specific strategies.
evaluation: Claims C51-C59 are well-supported by systematic comparisons between Experiments 1 and 2 (Figure 5A-D, Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2). The inference about strategy development (C59) is reasonable given the convergent evidence from reading speed, model predictions, and attention effects, though the specific mechanisms remain unspecified.

result: Native readers (Experiment 3) read faster (506±155 words/min) than L2 readers (Experiment 2) with comparable accuracy. Task modulation of reading time was significant but weaker for native readers, with layout effects dominating gaze duration and word/task features dominating rereading.
evaluation: Claims C60-C70 are supported by comprehensive comparisons between Experiments 2 and 3 (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1B-2B). The differential processing patterns between native and L2 readers are well-documented, though the interpretation about processing efficiency (C70) involves some speculation about underlying mechanisms.

result: During general-purpose reading without a question (Experiment 4), reading speed was slower (225±40 words/min) than goal-directed reading. Pre-trained and fine-tuned models showed similar predictive power, word reading time was predicted by layout and word features but not question relevance, and question-type-specific effects were absent, confirming task-dependence of goal-directed attention.
evaluation: Claims C71-C78 provide strong evidence for task-dependent attention through systematic comparison with Experiments 1-3 (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1C-2B). The absence of question relevance effects (C74, C77) and question-type differences (C76) in the control condition validates the task-specific nature of effects observed in goal-directed reading.

result: Human attention distribution during goal-directed reading is explained by task-optimized transformer DNN attention weights, while general-purpose reading is explained by word-prediction-optimized models. Text features modulate first-pass reading while question relevance modulates rereading, especially for L2 readers.
evaluation: Claims C79-C82 synthesize the main findings across all experiments. These summary claims are well-supported by the extensive empirical evidence from model comparisons, eye-tracking analyses, and cross-experiment comparisons, though they represent high-level interpretations of the data.

result: In DNNs, basic text features modulate attention weights in shallow layers while question relevance modulates deep layers, with both contributing to prediction of human reading time, reflecting hierarchical attention control for task optimization.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by layer-wise regression analyses (Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The parallel between DNN layer hierarchy and human temporal processing stages provides computational support for hierarchical attention control, though the mechanistic correspondence requires careful interpretation.

result: Pre-training on word prediction tasks produces text-based attention explaining general-purpose reading (Experiment 4), while fine-tuning on reading comprehension produces goal-directed attention explaining task-specific reading (Experiments 1-3).
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by systematic model comparisons across experiments (Figures 4B and 5A). The differential predictive power of pre-trained vs. fine-tuned models across task conditions provides strong evidence for training-induced attention specialization.

result: Pre-training on word prediction tasks enables models to learn statistical regularities including word surprisal, which modulates human reading time. Tokenization processes also contribute to similarity between human and DNN attention by allocating more attention to longer words.
evaluation: Claims C88-C94 provide mechanistic explanations for DNN-human correspondence, supported by citations to model development literature (C88-C89), reading research (C91), and neuroscience (C92). The explanations about surprisal (C90) and tokenization (C93-C94) are reasonable inferences about model properties, though direct empirical validation in this study is limited.

result: Previous reading models (E-Z reader, SWIFT) predict eye movements based on text features and optimization principles. Recent work showed RNN models can capture goal-directed attention for simple word-matching tasks, but the current study demonstrates that transformer models better capture attention for complex questions requiring inference.
evaluation: Claims C95-C100 accurately characterize prior work (supported by citations C95-C98) and position the current findings (C99-C100, supported by Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The comparison to prior models is appropriate and well-documented.

result: Previous studies showed inconsistent results about whether readers spend more time on task-relevant information, potentially due to working memory and topic familiarity. The current study confirms that L2 readers spend more time on question-relevant information than native readers, possibly because skilled readers process efficiently without extra encoding time.
evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are supported by citations and experimental data (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B). However, C104 is explicitly speculative about mechanisms ("it is possible that"), and alternative explanations for native-L2 differences (e.g., covert attention, different strategies) are not empirically tested in this study.

result: Previous studies showed mixed results about DNN attention interpretability and correlation with human reading time. The current results suggest this inconsistency may arise because deep layers are tuned to task relevance (which weakly affects native readers) while shallow layers capture text features (which reliably affect all readers).
evaluation: Claims C105-C109 accurately characterize conflicting prior findings (supported by citations). Claims C110-C113 provide a coherent explanation based on the current study's layer-wise analyses and native-L2 comparisons. The explanation is reasonable but represents a post-hoc interpretation that would benefit from direct testing.

result: Task-optimized transformer models automatically generate human-like attention without prior knowledge of human reading processes. Simpler models that fail at the task also fail to predict attention. The dataset and methods provide a probe for testing biological plausibility of NLP models, though human-like attention may not be a unique solution.
evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are well-supported by the systematic model comparisons throughout the study. Claims C116-C118 acknowledge limitations and broader implications appropriately. C116 is explicitly speculative but reasonable, while C117-C118 discuss methodological contributions that are supported by the demonstrated utility of the approach.

result: The study used 800 question/passage pairs from the RACE dataset, with six question types (three local, three global) that could not be answered by simple word matching. Participants were high-proficiency L2 readers (Experiments 1-2, 4) or native readers (Experiment 3) who were confident about their answers (90.47% confident, mean rating 3.25/4).
evaluation: Claims C119-C124 describe the experimental materials and participants, supported by data presentation and participant screening criteria. The confidence ratings (C123-C124) validate that participants were engaged and capable of performing the task, supporting the validity of the behavioral data.
